notes: Chapter 11 drills (hotels). Numeric answers verified by tests/test_drills.py against drill_checks_ch11.py. All facts hypothetical unless a source ID (references/sources_ch11.md) is cited.

drills.title: What one occupancy point is worth
drills.question: A 132-room hotel runs 72% occupancy at a $150 ADR. Compute RevPAR, the annual rooms revenue in one occupancy point, and the value of that point at 52% NOI flow-through (occupancy-led) and a 9% cap rate.
common_mistakes: Using rate-led flow-through (about 75%) for an occupancy gain
Treating one point as 1% of revenue (it is 1/72 = 1.39% of rooms revenue here)
drills.intuition: Occupancy points are room-nights; their value depends on the variable cost of servicing each extra guest.
drills.takeaway: A single occupancy point on a 132-room hotel is worth about $0.4 million of value; small share changes matter.

drills.title: Penetration indices
drills.question: Subject: 71% occupancy, $158.50 ADR. Comp set: 73%, $150.00. Compute MPI, ARI and RGI.
common_mistakes: Computing RGI as MPI + ARI - 100 (an approximation that drifts as indices move away from 100)
Reading RGI above 100 as success without checking its trend
drills.intuition: The hotel is buying rate with occupancy share; RGI shows the net revenue effect.
drills.takeaway: Report the RGI trend, not RevPAR growth, when judging the operator (Example 11.1).

drills.title: The EBITDA cap-rate trap
drills.question: An owner capitalizes EBITDA of $1,257,835 at a 9% cap. Market cap rates are quoted on NOI after a 4% FF&E reserve; total revenue is $5,463,612. Compute NOI, the correct value, and the owner's overstatement.
common_mistakes: Deducting the reserve from value instead of from income
Applying the reserve to rooms revenue only
drills.intuition: A cap rate belongs to a line. The error equals the capitalized reserve.
drills.takeaway: Always ask: cap rate on which line, after what reserve?

drills.title: RevPAR up, NOI down
drills.question: An operator reports RevPAR +6% and NOI -17% for the year. Give four plausible explanations and the report you would request to test each.

rubric: Channel mix: occupancy bought through OTAs or discount channels (channel-contribution report, commissions by channel)
Occupancy-led growth with lower flow-through than rate-led (occupancy/ADR split; CPOR trend)
Labor cost inflation: wages, overtime, benefits (payroll by department, hours per occupied room)
Fixed-charge increases: property-tax reassessment, insurance renewal (tax bill, policy)
Undistributed cost growth or one-off items (A&G, POM, utilities detail)
States that RevPAR is a revenue measure and NOI is the owner's line; does not accept the RevPAR headline as value creation

drills.solution: See Case 11.1. Build a sequential bridge from Year 1 NOI to Year 2 NOI, changing one driver at a time, and classify each step as structural or fixable.
common_mistakes: Accepting 'RevPAR beat budget' as evidence of performance
Blaming 'costs' without a bridge
drills.intuition: Revenue can be bought; profit cannot.
drills.takeaway: Ask for flow-through and a bridge before discussing value.

drills.title: Flow-through with the wrong sign
drills.question: Total revenue rose from $4,421,172 to $4,688,698. GOP fell from $1,945,272 to $1,885,459 and NOI from $953,626 to $790,516. Compute GOP and NOI flow-through.
common_mistakes: Computing margin change instead of flow-through
Dividing by the new revenue rather than the change
drills.intuition: Negative flow-through means costs grew faster than revenue; the growth was bought or costs inflated.
drills.takeaway: Flow-through is the first number to ask for when revenue and profit diverge.

drills.title: Take the group?
drills.question: A 250-room hotel (20 contract rooms nightly) is offered a 120-room, two-night group at $175 with $60 banquet spend per room-night at a 35% margin. Transient demand is forecast at 190 rooms per night at $235 with a 15% acquisition cost. CPOR $40; fees 10% of rooms revenue. Compute displaced rooms per night, the net contribution of accepting, and the break-even group rate. Decide.

rubric: Compares contribution, not revenue
Includes banquet profit and channel costs
States the decision is conditional on the transient forecast and names the demand level that reverses it
Proposes protections (cutoff, attrition, F&B minimum) or alternate dates

drills.solution: Displaced = 190 - (250 - 20 - 120) = 80. Group = 240 x (157.50 - 40 + 21) = $33,240. Displaced = 160 x (176.25 - 40) = $21,800. Net +$11,440. Break-even: 240 x (0.9r - 19) = 21,800 -> r = $122.04. Accept, with cutoff and attrition protection.
common_mistakes: Comparing group revenue with transient revenue
Ignoring that displacement depends on a forecast
drills.intuition: Groups bring banquets and cheaper distribution; transient brings rate.
drills.takeaway: Revenue management outputs a minimum rate conditional on demand, not a yes or no.

drills.title: Break-even occupancy after a wage shock
drills.question: 150 rooms, ADR $128, other revenue 3% of rooms, CPOR $26.80, revenue-variable costs 21%, fixed costs $1,712,500, debt service $1,040,842. Break-even occupancy before and after debt service?
common_mistakes: Forgetting other revenue
Holding ADR fixed in a downturn stress without saying so
drills.intuition: Break-even is fixed costs over contribution per room.
drills.takeaway: See Case 11.6: the wage shock moved break-even up 4 points.

drills.title: When does the incentive fee pay?
drills.question: Total revenue $22.0m (hold it constant). Base fee 3%; tax and insurance $1.55m; reserve 4%; incentive fee 20% of ACF above an 8% priority on $52m. Compute the incentive fee at GOP of $4.2m, $7.04m and $8.82m.
common_mistakes: Applying the incentive rate to all of ACF
Forgetting that the base fee and reserve come out before the priority test
drills.intuition: The incentive fee is a call option on ACF struck at the owner's priority.

drills.title: PIP-adjusted bid
drills.question: Stabilized NOI $1.55m at a 9.0% cap. PIP $2.34m, 15% contingency, displacement $260,000, carry $150,000, 15% required profit on PIP capital. Compute stabilized value, the PIP-adjusted price, and price per key (130 rooms).
common_mistakes: Doing the PIP at cost (no required profit)
Deducting the PIP without contingency or displacement
drills.intuition: Renovation capital is risk capital and must earn a return.
drills.takeaway: Use sdesk.hotel.pip_adjusted_price; see Case 11.8 and Case D.

drills.title: Size the hotel loan
drills.question: T-12 NOI $2.15m; appraised value $27,428,571; 7.50% rate, 25-year amortization. Hotel lender: 60% LTV, 1.50x DSCR, 12% debt yield. Compute each constraint and the loan.
common_mistakes: Sizing on pro forma NOI
Using the annual rate without monthly amortization in the constant
drills.intuition: Hotel lenders lend on trailing cash flow and demand larger cushions.
drills.takeaway: See Example 11.4: about $3m less than a multifamily lender would lend on the same NOI.

drills.title: April 2020: occupancy or rate?

inputs.note: April 2020 levels from STR (ch11-S04); prior-year levels implied from STR's reported changes (-63.9% occupancy, -44.4% ADR) and rounded

drills.question: STR reported April 2020 U.S. occupancy of 24.5% and ADR of $73.23, with occupancy down 63.9% and ADR down 44.4% year over year. Using implied April 2019 levels of 67.8% and $131.71, compute the RevPAR change and the share of the (log) RevPAR decline due to occupancy. What does this imply for break-even analysis?

rubric: Computes RevPAR change near -80% (STR reported -79.9%)
Uses logs so the shares add to 100%
Notes ADR also fell sharply, so break-even occupancy at pre-shock ADR is optimistic
Distinguishes the reported figures [FACT] from the implied prior-year levels [INFERENCE]

drills.solution: RevPAR: (0.245 x 73.23)/(0.678 x 131.71) - 1 = -79.9%. ln(0.245/0.678) = -1.018; ln(1 - 0.799) = -1.606; occupancy share = 63.4%, ADR share 36.6%. A break-even computed at the old ADR understates the occupancy needed.
common_mistakes: Adding percentage changes (-63.9% + -44.4%)
Treating implied prior-year levels as published facts
drills.intuition: In a demand collapse, occupancy falls first and hardest, but rate follows.

drills.title: The BOV you should not sign
drills.question: A servicer wants a firm value in 24 hours for a 100-room hotel. The borrower's T-12 shows RevPAR $104; the STR report shows $92 for the same period. The franchise expires in 14 months with no PIP letter, and the tax bill predates a sale three years ago. What do you deliver?

rubric: Quantifies the discrepancy: $438,000 of rooms revenue, about $3.5m of value at 75% flow-through and 9.5%
Lists explanations (non-room revenue in rooms, occupancy taxes, period or room-count differences, STR errors, overstatement) and the documents that resolve each
Treats the franchise expiry and PIP as a second independent value driver
Declines a point value; delivers a conditional range and a diligence list with a date for a firm value
Abstention from a point estimate is the best answer

drills.solution: See Problem 11.10. The right deliverable is a conditional range and a reconciliation plan; the wrong deliverable is a confident number.
common_mistakes: Averaging the two RevPAR figures
Assuming STR is always right
drills.intuition: When two data sources disagree by more than the valuation tolerance, the value is not yet knowable.
drills.takeaway: Abstention from a point value is a professional output, not a failure.

drills.title: Flag or no flag
drills.question: Renewing the flag: stabilized NOI $949,090 at an 8.75% cap, PIP $2.24m. Going independent: NOI $647,867 at 9.5%, capex $0.70m. Compute value net of capital for each and the difference (ignore ramp-up).
common_mistakes: Comparing fee percentages instead of NOI after fees and demand
Using the same cap rate for both
drills.intuition: Fees buy demand; compare NOI after both.
drills.takeaway: Independence needs an RGI near 103 to compete in Case 11.3.

drills.title: Seasonal working capital
drills.question: Monthly cash flow after debt service (Jan-Dec) is given. Compute the working-capital reserve needed if peak-season surplus stays with the owner, and the equity needed if a cash trap sweeps every positive month to the lender.
drills.solution: Without trap: largest peak-to-trough fall in cumulative cash = Sep-Feb deficit = $1,359,081. With trap: sum of negative months = $1,489,929.
common_mistakes: Using annual cash flow (+$667,361) and concluding no reserve is needed
Starting the cumulative sum in January, which hides the Sep-Dec deficit
drills.intuition: Annual ratios hide monthly cash; covenants decide who keeps the summer cash.
drills.takeaway: Size reserves from monthly cash flow (Case 11.5).

drills.title: Investment committee: sell now or after the PIP
drills.question: Using Case 11.8's facts, compute the owner's net proceeds from selling now, the expected PV of renovating and selling in two years, and the difference. Then present a recommendation to the committee with conditions and the facts that would reverse it.

rubric: Prices the sale with contingency, displacement, carry and required profit
Computes scenario PVs and the expected value, and the bad-case shortfall (about $0.86m)
States the break-even exit cap (about 9.39%) and the liquidity needed to fund the PIP
Recommends conditionally; identifies negotiable buyer deductions (about $135,000 per 5 points of contingency or profit)
Names facts that reverse the decision (fixed-price bid, loan maturity, thin buyer pool)

drills.solution: Sell now: price $13,717,572, net $13,374,633. Hold: PVs 14,525,259 / 13,955,543 / 12,517,369; expected $13,867,309; advantage $492,676 with a one-in-five chance of being $857,264 worse off. Renovate only if the owner has the liquidity and a view of exit caps inside 9.39%.
common_mistakes: Comparing the buyer's price with stabilized value
Ignoring the overrun and cap-rate risk the owner keeps by renovating
drills.intuition: Selling before a PIP transfers renovation risk and renovation profit together.
drills.takeaway: Timing decisions compare risky streams, not prices.
